documents.title: AI for Students
tiers: Policies vary by instructor, course and assignment; no tier system
documents.summary: Student-facing page on using AI to learn: it welcomes experimentation and study uses, warns about reliability, and says course policies differ and may restrict AI heavily. Students are told to ask the instructor when unsure.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no rule of its own: "AI usage policies differ between instructors, courses and assignments" and "Unsure about AI usage? Ask your instructor!" leave the decision to instructors, while "Experiment extensively with AI tools" encourages learning use, so delegates.

units.why: Tells students to "Experiment extensively with AI tools to learn and solve problems", so AI exploration is welcomed by default for learning; P02 fits since it encourages use, with the policy-compliance clause coded separately.
units.anchor: Experiment extensively with AI tools to learn and solve problems

units.why: "keeping NC State academic policies and procedures in mind" ties AI use to existing university rules; P77 (comply with existing policy) fits, not P45 which treats AI as a collaborator.
units.anchor: keeping NC State academic policies and procedures in mind
units.policy: Students keep NC State academic policies and procedures in mind when using AI tools.

units.why: "Know which tools are available and which tools are not" points students to approved versus rejected tools; P50 (prefer vetted tools) is the nearest type.
units.anchor: Know which tools are available and which tools are not.
units.fit_note: The type is about data protection; this unit only says to know which university-approved tools are available.

units.why: "Focus on familiar subjects to better understand AI's strengths and weaknesses" advises how to learn to judge AI output; P31 (verify output) fits only partly.
units.anchor: Focus on familiar subjects to better understand AI's strengths and weaknesses.
units.fit_note: Advises practicing on familiar subjects so students can spot AI strengths and weaknesses, rather than saying to verify output.

units.why: "Many scholarly sources and current academic journals are missing from the tool's datasets" is a caution about AI as a search tool; it warns of unreliable output, closest to P31.
units.anchor: Many scholarly sources and current academic journals are missing from the tool's datasets.
units.fit_note: States a limitation (missing scholarly sources) as fact rather than telling students to verify.

units.why: "The tool cannot critically evaluate information or distinguish reliable sources" warns that chatbots lack understanding; fits P31 as a reason to evaluate output critically.
units.anchor: The tool cannot critically evaluate information or distinguish reliable sources.

units.why: "Be aware of the tool's tendency to invent information" directly names hallucination, so P31 fits.
units.anchor: Be aware of the tool's tendency to invent information.

units.why: "Summaries (like abstracts) can aid prioritization and initial comprehension" permits AI summaries as a starting point, a study aid under P14.
units.anchor: Summaries (like abstracts) can aid prioritization and initial comprehension.

units.why: "Writing your notes significantly improves long-term understanding" gives the learning reason for not outsourcing note-taking; P41 fits.
units.anchor: Writing your notes significantly improves long-term understanding.

units.why: "Use AI to generate quizzes, not just summaries" recommends AI-made quizzes for retrieval practice, which is P14.
units.anchor: Use AI to generate quizzes, not just summaries.

units.why: "Utilize LLMs to create practice questions for active learning and retrieval practice" is a recommended study use, P14.
units.anchor: Utilize LLMs to create practice questions for active learning and retrieval practice.

units.why: "Employ LLMs as a study aid, not a replacement for core materials and reliable sources" allows AI as a study aid; P14 is nearest though it also limits AI to supplementary use.
units.anchor: Employ LLMs as a study aid, not a replacement for core materials and reliable sources.
units.fit_note: Also says AI must not replace core materials and reliable sources.

units.why: "Use LLMs to spark discussion and debate, not just passively accept summaries" recommends AI as an interlocutor; P12 (tutor-like understanding) fits only partly.
units.anchor: Use LLMs to spark discussion and debate, not just passively accept summaries.
units.fit_note: Frames AI as a partner for discussion and debate, not a tutor explaining concepts.

units.why: "Using AI for assignments may be heavily restricted by course policies" says restriction is set by courses, so P04 (instructor decides) fits.
units.anchor: Using AI for assignments may be heavily restricted by course policies.

units.why: "Direct problem-solving and writing are crucial for skill development" gives the reason for limiting AI on assignments; P41.
units.anchor: Direct problem-solving and writing are crucial for skill development.

units.why: "Receiving and responding to questions improves writing more effectively than direct editing" is a learning-based reason about how to use AI for writing; nearest is P41 although it is about prose feedback.
units.anchor: Receiving and responding to questions improves writing more effectively than direct editing.
units.fit_note: Implies that AI should ask questions rather than directly edit student writing; this is a prose-specific use guideline.

units.why: "Most courses emphasize developing a strong foundation before advanced tool use" is a fundamentals-first rationale (P42).
units.anchor: Most courses emphasize developing a strong foundation before advanced tool use.

units.why: "AI usage policies differ between instructors, courses and assignments" states that the rule is set per instructor, course and assignment: P04.
units.anchor: AI usage policies differ between instructors, courses and assignments.

units.why: "These policies aim to help you master fundamental and advanced skills" explains the purpose of course AI policies as protecting learning; P41.
units.anchor: These policies aim to help you master fundamental and advanced skills within your field.

units.why: "Unsure about AI usage? Ask your instructor!" is exactly P10 (ask before using AI).
units.anchor: Unsure about AI usage? Ask your instructor!

units.why: Directs students to LinkedIn Learning AI courses ("you can find courses on LinkedIn Learning that challenge and inform you"), which is AI-literacy training offered to students: P70.
units.anchor: you can find courses on LinkedIn Learning that challenge and inform you
units.policy: The university points students to LinkedIn Learning courses on the fundamentals, applications or ethics of AI.

documents.title: Developing Course AI Guidelines & Driving Class AI Discussion
tiers: AI use as a learning aid
AI use as a collaborative tool
documents.summary: DELTA article that tells instructors to write course- and assignment-level AI guidelines and offers three sample statements (restricting, learning aid, collaborative). It states there is no official university AI policy and suggests class discussion of ethics.
documents.stance_why: It says "there is no official university policy regarding AI use" and gives instructors three sample statements to adapt (restricting, learning aid, collaborative), so the document sets no stance itself and delegates with tiers.

units.why: "It is important to provide students with guidance on how you expect them to use AI tools in your course" asks instructors to state expectations: P09.
units.anchor: It is important to provide students with guidance on how you expect them to use

units.why: "You should design concrete, actionable instructions for students on how and when they can use AI" tells instructors to set course-level rules; P09 (state expectations) rather than P04 because it requires writing the rules down.
units.anchor: You should design concrete, actionable instructions for students on how and when they can use

units.why: "This could be a good opportunity to discuss AI use and expectations with students and design the procedures together" suggests co-creating the policy: P67.
units.anchor: discuss AI use and expectations with students and design the procedures together

units.why: "clearly specify how AI may or may not be used in coursework, assignments, and assessments" asks for explicit statements in the course: P09.
units.anchor: clearly specify how AI may or may not be used in coursework, assignments, and assessments

units.why: "provide examples and directions on how students should document and share their use of AI" asks instructors to set up a disclosure practice; P24 fits only partly because the actor is the instructor.
units.anchor: provide examples and directions on how students should document and share their use of AI
units.policy: Instructors provide examples and directions on how students should document and share their use of AI with peers and the instructor, at the course level and ideally at the assignment level.
units.fit_note: The rule addresses instructors who should set up documentation guidance, not students' disclosure duty itself.

units.why: "align any statement with the same spirit of academic integrity" ties course AI statements to the existing integrity policy: P77.
units.anchor: align any statement with the same spirit of academic integrity

units.why: "there is no official university policy regarding AI use" states that the university sets no AI rule, leaving it to courses: P04.
units.anchor: there is no official university policy regarding AI use
units.fit_note: Records the absence of a university-wide policy rather than a delegation instruction.

units.why: "Assignment-level guidance is often more helpful to students" recommends setting rules per assignment, P04.
units.anchor: Assignment-level guidance is often more helpful to students.

units.why: "please review the approved AI tools and data sensitivity levels" tells instructors to use vetted tools and respect data sensitivity: P50.
units.anchor: please review the approved AI tools and data sensitivity levels

units.why: Says statements "were adapted from conversations with a variety of generative AI tools", an instructor-side use of AI to draft materials: P59 describes this, and the statement is a disclosure.
units.anchor: adapted from conversations with a variety of generative AI tools

units.why: "You may want to consider having policies/statements for each assignment rather than an overall policy" lets instructors set rules per assignment: P04.
units.anchor: consider having policies/statements for each assignment rather than an overall policy

units.why: "Some instructors simply consider AI use to fall under the general academic integrity guidelines" describes treating AI under existing integrity rules, closest to P45.
units.anchor: Some instructors simply consider AI use to fall under the
units.fit_note: Treats AI under general integrity rules, not specifically as a human collaborator.

units.why: In the restricting sample: "You are not allowed to use any artificial intelligence (AI) tools" bans AI on all assignments, so P01; it is a sample statement for instructors to adopt.
units.anchor: You are not allowed to use any artificial intelligence (AI) tools

units.why: "Any attempt to use these tools will be considered academic misconduct" classifies prohibited AI use as misconduct: P36.
units.anchor: Any attempt to use these tools will be considered academic misconduct

units.why: "Students are expected to complete all work independently and without the assistance of AI-generated content" repeats the ban in terms of submitting only own work, so P19.
units.anchor: complete all work independently and without the assistance of AI-generated content

units.why: "please consult with the instructor before submitting your work" about acceptable use: P10 (ask before using).
units.anchor: please consult with the instructor before submitting your work

units.why: "This course permits you to use artificial intelligence (AI) tools" opens the learning-aid sample with permission, P02 (permit by default under conditions).
units.anchor: This course permits you to use artificial intelligence (AI) tools

units.why: "AI is more like your tutor or TA, not a replacement for your independent thinking" casts AI as a tutor: P12 (tutor, not producing work).
units.anchor: AI is more like your tutor or TA, not a replacement for your independent thinking.

units.why: "Not use AI tools to replace your own thinking or analysis or to avoid engaging with the course content" means students stay the primary thinker: P32.
units.anchor: Not use AI tools to replace your own thinking or analysis

units.why: "Cite or explain any AI tools you use" requires attribution of AI use: P24.
units.anchor: Cite or explain any AI tools you use.

units.why: "Provide the name of the AI tool, the date of access, the URL of the interface, and the specific prompt" lists the citation details: P25.
units.anchor: the name of the AI tool, the date of access, the URL of the interface,

units.why: "Explain what you learned from the AI tool, how you verified its accuracy" asks for a written reflection on AI use: P26.
units.anchor: Explain what you learned from the AI tool, how you verified its accuracy and reliability
units.fit_note: Asks for an explanation within the submission rather than keeping transcripts or logs.

units.why: "You are accountable for any mistakes or errors made by the AI tool" makes students responsible for AI errors: P29.
units.anchor: You are accountable for any mistakes or errors made by the AI tool.

units.why: "Always check and edit the output before submitting your work" requires verifying AI output: P31.
units.anchor: Always check and edit the output before submitting your work.

units.why: "notify the instructor immediately and correct them" if errors are found after submission; a duty to report an AI-related problem, so P71 only partly.
units.anchor: notify the instructor immediately and correct them as soon as possible
units.fit_note: The duty is to report and correct AI output errors found after submission, not data exposure or misconduct.

units.why: "is considered a form of academic dishonesty" classifies uncited or unverified AI use as dishonesty: P36.
units.anchor: is considered a form of academic dishonesty

units.why: "will result in a zero grade for the assignment and possible disciplinary action" states a concrete penalty: P37.
units.anchor: will result in a zero grade for the assignment and possible disciplinary action

units.why: The NOTE "Some instructors will also list specific acceptable and unacceptable uses" says instructors decide the detail of permitted uses: P04.
units.anchor: Some instructors will also list specific acceptable and unacceptable uses

units.why: "students are encouraged to explore and utilize generative AI tools" opens the collaborative sample with encouragement: P02.
units.anchor: students are encouraged to explore and utilize generative AI tools

units.why: "valuable for brainstorming, drafting, and enhancing your understanding of the material" lists uses; P15 (brainstorming) is the nearest though it also names drafting.
units.anchor: valuable for brainstorming, drafting, and enhancing your understanding of the material
units.fit_note: Also names drafting and understanding course material.

units.why: "critically assess and cite any AI-generated content used in your assignments and projects" combines evaluation and citation; coded P24 for citation.
units.anchor: critically assess and cite any AI-generated content used in your assignments and projects
units.fit_note: Also requires students to critically assess AI content (P31).

units.why: "Students are expected to demonstrate their own understanding and critical thinking in their final submissions" keeps students the thinker: P32.
units.anchor: demonstrate their own understanding and critical thinking in their final submissions

units.why: "We may also integrate AI Tools into some of our assignments" signals redesigned assignments that use AI: P35 (redesign assignments around AI).
units.anchor: We may also integrate AI Tools into some of our assignments.

units.why: "Use AI tools only for tasks that are appropriate for your level of learning and understanding" limits AI by learner level; P42 (protect novices) is nearest.
units.anchor: Use AI tools only for tasks that are appropriate for your level of learning and

units.why: Gives an APA citation example for ChatGPT; the example shows the form of a citation including tool, version and URL: P25.
units.anchor: OpenAI. (2024). ChatGPT (Mar 14 version) [Large language model].

units.why: "Do not rely on the AI tool to produce flawless or correct results" warns AI can be wrong, P31.
units.anchor: Do not rely on the AI tool to produce flawless or correct results.

units.why: "discuss the use of AI tools with your group members and agree on how you plan to use them" sets a group-level agreement and transparency with the instructor; no type covers it.
units.anchor: discuss the use of AI tools with your group members and agree on how you
units.uncovered_note: For group assignments, team members must discuss and agree on their AI use and how to be transparent about it with the instructor.

units.why: "Do you want to ask students to verify or check sources of information used by an AI tool" prompts instructors to consider a verification rule: P31.
units.anchor: Do you want to ask students to verify or check sources of information used by
units.fit_note: Framed as a question for instructors to consider.

units.why: "Do you want to ask students to consider representation in any AI responses" prompts instructors about bias in AI output: P53.
units.anchor: consider representation in any AI responses that they use in their work
units.fit_note: Framed as a question for instructors to consider.

units.why: "Do you want students to acknowledge, cite or share AI use" prompts the instructor to decide on disclosure: P24.
units.anchor: Do you want students to acknowledge, cite or share AI use
units.fit_note: Framed as a question for instructors to consider.

units.why: "Try out AI each semester ... It's helpful to understand how students can use it on assignments before you design guidelines" tells instructors to learn AI before setting policy: P63.
units.anchor: Try out AI each semester as it continues to improve and develop

units.why: Lists UMN's "Different “levels” of AI use from encouraged to limiting to prohibiting" as an example, which is a tiered scheme: P05.
units.anchor: Different “levels” of AI use from encouraged to limiting to prohibiting

units.why: "Consider summarizing for students at the beginning of the semester some of the positive uses of generative AI and some of the negatives" asks instructors to explain and discuss AI with students: P66.
units.anchor: Consider summarizing for students at the beginning of the semester some of the positive uses

units.why: "Gender and Racial Bias in AI" is listed as a concerning aspect to raise with students, P53.
units.anchor: Gender and Racial Bias in AI

units.why: "copyright or intellectual property concerns with how AI systems are trained" lists IP as a concern to discuss: P52.
units.anchor: copyright or intellectual property concerns with how AI systems are

units.why: "Lack of basic skill development" is named as a concern about AI, linked to skill-building: P41.
units.anchor: Lack of basic skill development

units.why: "Consider having a discussion with students and creating some course norms and guidelines together" recommends co-creating course norms: P67.
units.anchor: Consider having a discussion with students and creating some course norms and guidelines together.

units.why: "Conduct a structured debate where students present their points and counter-arguments" is an in-class activity to discuss AI use: P66.
units.anchor: Conduct a structured debate where students present their points and counter-arguments.

documents.unit: Graduate School Handbook 3.6 Theses and Dissertations
documents.title: Graduate Handbook: Artificial Intelligence Policy for Dissertations and Theses
documents.summary: Graduate Handbook section on AI in theses and dissertations. AI use is allowed provided students document it clearly in the thesis and Authorship Statement, with advice on privacy, bias, detectors and advisor discussion.
documents.stance_why: The guiding principle is "Candidates utilizing GAI tools must document their use clearly and thoroughly", with "The mere use of LLMs does not constitute plagiarism", so use is allowed on condition of documentation: permit.

units.why: The Overview states "The goal of this document is to propose a framework to allow our graduate students to use these tools ethically", an institution-level framework for AI in theses: P56.
units.anchor: propose a framework to allow our graduate students to use these tools ethically

units.why: "Our students would benefit from receiving training on how to use GAI tools efficiently, ethically and reliably" supports AI training for students: P70.
units.anchor: Our students would benefit from receiving training on how to use GAI tools efficiently, ethically

units.why: "The mere use of LLMs does not constitute plagiarism" makes use permissible in theses; closest is P62 (AI in research and scholarship).
units.anchor: The mere use of LLMs does not constitute plagiarism

units.why: "the uninformed and/or poorly documented inclusion of outputs from LLMs into dissertations and theses may constitute a form of plagiarism" classes poorly documented AI use as plagiarism: P36.
units.anchor: poorly documented inclusion of outputs from LLMs into dissertations and theses may constitute a form

units.why: "Candidates utilizing GAI tools must document their use clearly and thoroughly in their dissertation or thesis" is the Graduate School's guiding disclosure rule: P24.
units.anchor: Candidates utilizing GAI tools must document their use clearly and thoroughly in their dissertation or

units.why: "discuss ... acceptable use of LLMs or other GAI tools as early as practically possible with their advisor" asks students to settle the rule with the advisor first: P10.
units.anchor: acceptable use of LLMs or other GAI tools as early as practically possible with their
units.fit_note: Asks for an early discussion with the advisor, not only when unsure.

units.why: "Advisors need to be direct and transparent about what tools students are permitted to use, and about the reasons for any restrictions" asks advisors to state their rules and reasons: P09.
units.anchor: Advisors need to be direct and transparent about what tools students are permitted to use
units.fit_note: Applies to advisors of theses, not to syllabi, and also asks for reasons (P66).

units.why: Program rules, "if such principles are adopted by the program, they must be clearly communicated to the students and applied uniformly by advisory committees", add program-level rules that must be communicated: P09.
units.anchor: they must be clearly communicated to the students and applied uniformly by advisory committees
units.fit_note: Also requires uniform application of program-level principles by advisory committees.

units.why: "GAI tools raise issues of privacy and intellectual property" names privacy and IP concerns with AI tools: P50.
units.anchor: GAI tools raise issues of privacy and intellectual property.

units.why: "Material submitted can become part of the application's database, user's information may be collected and cookies installed" explains data risks of AI tools: P50.
units.anchor: Material submitted can become part of the application's database

units.why: "LLMs are models; therefore, there are inherent biases associated with them. Users must, at a minimum, be aware" names bias as a concern: P53.
units.anchor: there are inherent biases associated with them. Users must, at a minimum, be aware

units.why: "the use of AI tools claiming to detect LLM generated text is discouraged" because of "unreliable nature": P39.
units.anchor: the use of AI tools claiming to detect LLM generated text is discouraged

units.why: "no LLM tool should be credited as co-author on a research paper" is a rule on authorship in scholarship: P62.

units.why: "does not directly address the use of GAI in generic courses" limits the scope of the section to dissertations and theses: P61.
units.anchor: The above guiding principle does not directly address the use of GAI in generic courses.
units.fit_note: States what the policy does not cover and refers to OFE and DELTA pages for courses.

units.why: "The use of writing assistance tools such as Grammarly is generally allowed and rarely acknowledged" gives a prose-tool rule: P18.
units.anchor: The use of writing assistance tools such as Grammarly is generally allowed and rarely acknowledged.

units.why: "If in doubt, students should contact their advisory committee and/or err on the side of caution and acknowledge use" is P10 (ask first) combined with disclosure when unsure.

units.why: "Approval of the Authorship Statement by the advisory committee is a necessary condition for passing the final oral examination" makes the AI description reviewable by the committee; no disclosure type covers committee approval, so P62.
units.anchor: Approval of the Authorship Statement by the advisory committee is a necessary condition for passing

notes: Coder B. Three included university-layer documents coded; no school, computing or course documents exist in the collect file. The DELTA page contains sample statements written for instructors to adopt, so unit actors for samples are the student while the document is instructor guidance. The grad handbook section covers only theses and dissertations.
